steps: Bend the index and middle fingers of both hands downward at the knuckles, keeping the other fingers folded down.
Hold your non-dominant bent-V hand still in front of your chest without moving it.
Sweep your dominant bent-V hand downward and past the non-dominant hand in one motion.
Keep the base hand frozen as the base; only the dominant hand does the moving.
Some signers use a palm-down S hand as the base while the dominant bent-V hand strikes a glancing blow off its top.
tip: Lifeprint glosses this production HARD, tough, and difficult; for hard-as-in-a-rock use the separate sign SOLID instead.

steps: Raise your dominant hand to shoulder height in front of you, steady and clearly visible.
Extend the index, middle, ring, and pinky fingers upward with a slight spread between them.
Fold your thumb across your palm and tuck it flat behind the four raised fingers.
Turn the palm to face forward so the reader sees the four fingers clearly.
Hold the hand still with a neutral face, since number signs carry no special facial grammar.
tip: Four fingers up with the thumb folded flat against the palm; Lifeprint's number lesson pairs this with the /numbers/4.svg illustration.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand still in front of your chest with the fingers extended and pointing upward.
Brush the fingertips of your open dominant hand upward along the non-dominant fingers.
Repeat the upward brush a second time, for two quick brushes in total.
Let the non-dominant fingers bend slightly as the dominant hand brushes past them.
Keep the movement light and quick; the non-dominant hand stays planted throughout.
tip: Two upward brushes mean easy; do it with a single brush and the sign becomes ALMOST — a difference Lifeprint flags in Lesson 32.

steps: Shape both hands into bent hands, curling all four fingers like claws while the thumbs stay relaxed.
Stack one bent hand on top of the other in front of your chest, as if laying a brick.
Lift the lower hand and stack it on top of the upper one, climbing upward step by step.
Keep climbing with alternating hands for three or four layers to show the rising structure.
Use all four fingers on each hand; this full-handed version marks the noun, a finished building.
tip: Four fingers per hand marks the noun BUILDING; the two-finger version marks the verb, the process of building, per Lifeprint.

steps: Sign SELL first, using the same production as the dictionary entry for Sell.
Add the AGENT person-affix immediately after the SELL sign without a pause.
Shape both hands into flat hands with the fingers together and extended.
Bring the two flat hands together in front of your chest at the same height.
Move both flat hands downward together in one smooth, decisive motion.
Keep your expression neutral; the affix turns the verb SELL into the noun seller.
tip: Lifeprint glosses this compound SELLER and SALESPERSON; in ASL the AGENT affix attaches to a verb to name the person doing the action.

steps: Hold both flat hands in front of your waist with the palms facing fully upward.
Sweep both palms forward and upward together in a smooth rising arc.
Ease the arc back down a little at the end, as if laying the offer on a table.
Keep the movement generous and open so the offering gesture reads clearly.
Face the person receiving the offer with an open, offering expression.
tip: Picture laying an offer on a table — the arc presents it to the other person; Lifeprint also glosses it propose, suggest, and recommend.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a flat B hand with the fingers together and extended.
Hold the B hand steady in front of your chest with the palm facing sideways.
Cross the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand into an R handshape.
Slide the R hand forward along the top edge of the stationary B hand.
Let the R hand drop off the end of the B hand and fall downward to finish.
tip: An initialized form of the sign END — the R hand does the same END slide; Lifeprint notes initialized signs are otherwise best avoided in ASL.

steps: Shape both hands into loose claw hands, the fingers curved as if cupping a ball.
Hold the curved hands up in front of your chest with the palms facing slightly forward.
Push both hands forward while twisting your palms slightly backward together.
Let the movement trace the curve of an imaginary ball held between the hands.
Keep your face neutral; plurality comes from context, so one sign covers one group or many.
tip: Lifeprint also glosses this sign CLUSTER or CATEGORY, and notes an initialized G version for naming the English word group directly.
